title: AA in Obesity and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD).
journal: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology
abstract: Obesity and MASLD (NAFLD) are chronic, low-grade systemic inflammatory diseases resulting from complex interactions among diet, adipose tissue, gut microbiota, liver, muscle, pancreas, and the brain. Central to this integrative framework are AA and other polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), which regulate inflammation, insulin sensitivity, neuroendocrine signaling, and energy homeostasis.Excess consumption of energy-dense foods rich in saturated and trans fats leads to adipocyte hypertrophy, altered membrane fluidity, increased antigenicity, and enhanced recruitment of macrophages and T cells into adipose tissue. These changes promote the sustained release of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, MIF, and CRP, contributing to insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and MASLD (NAFLD). In contrast, adequate availability of GLA, DGLA, AA, EPA, and DHA improves cell membrane dynamics and serves as a substrate for anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving lipid mediators, including lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, maresins, and nitrolipids, which suppress inflammatory signaling and enhance adiponectin production.Abdominal obesity can be considered a localized glucocorticoid excess state driven by increased adipose 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-1 (11β-HSD-1) activity, linking visceral fat accumulation to insulin resistance, altered PPAR signaling, and chronic inflammation. Suppression of 11β-HSD-1, increased PUFA intake, and exercise can ameliorate these abnormalities.Gut microbiota and their short-chain fatty acids influence inflammation, leptin signaling, incretin secretion, and lipid metabolism, while PUFAs-including AA-activate gut-brain-liver neural circuits via vagal pathways and G protein-coupled receptors to regulate satiety, insulin secretion, and hepatic glucose production. This chapter also emphasizes the role of hypothalamic factors, particularly BDNF, in integrating nutritional, hormonal, and inflammatory signals.In summary, AA and related PUFAs are critical modulators of inflammation resolution, neuroendocrine control, and metabolic balance, offering a unifying mechanistic framework for the prevention and management of obesity and its associated metabolic disorders.

title: Persistence and geographic availability of Medicare Part D coverage for non-diabetes GLP-1 therapies, 2024-2026.
Investigating GLP-1 sourcing preferences on social media and motivations for use: Survey with choice-based conjoint (CBC) exercise.
abstract: The growing use of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) drugs such as Ozempic for weight loss interventions has led to increased concerns about inappropriate use, supply shortages, and high-risk sourcing. However, little is known about the influence of online marketing strategies on purchasing preferences for GLP-1 products. This study uses a survey with a Choice-Based Conjoint (CBC) exercise to assess features of social media posts that are most influential for intent to purchase GLP-1 products and identify motivations for use. Participants were recruited based on current use of GLP-1 drugs, previous use, or considering use (n = 242). Utility scores from the conjoint analysis quantified the influence of tested features. Conjoint findings showed greater preference for posts that feature branded semaglutide (e.g., Wegovy)(15.38, SD = 45.29), display products in packaging (47.49, SD = 46.72), have accredited digital pharmacies as the seller (25.16, SD = 47.31) (e.g., Amazon Pharmacy), include medical endorsements for diabetes treatment (13.16, SD = 49.04), and offer a free consultation (13.18, SD = 32.00). Analysis was conducted on survey questions measuring GLP-1 purchasing channels and motivations for use. Over half of participants (51.7%) reported that social media content influenced their perceptions of GLP-1 drugs and 45.8% (n = 65) of GLP-1 users reported purchasing product from high-risk sources (i.e., personal network or individual sellers online). Exploratory analysis shows a possible association between self-reported high-risk sourcing and reliance on GLP-1s for medical conditions. Overall, our findings identify influential attributes of GLP-1 social media ads (i.e., branding and visual display of products) and suggests greater support is needed for online moderation efforts to prevent high-risk purchasing activity and increase safe access to GLP-1s for those with medical needs.

title: Type 2 diabetes and the cardio-renal-metabolic syndrome: The evolving roles of GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists.
abstract: The impact of type 2 diabetes (T2D) extends beyond mere management of blood glucose; it also encompasses related cardiovascular, renal and metabolic issues. This interconnected framework, known as the cardio-renal-metabolic (CRM) syndrome, calls for a shift in therapeutic approach. While traditional treatments have made progress focusing on glucose management, a residual risk still exists for conditions such as atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, heart failure and obesity. The 2025 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care now emphasize treatment algorithms based on risk and complication management, prioritizing comorbidities associated with the CRM syndrome rather than solely focusing on glucose management. This article consolidates current evidence, mechanistic insights and clinical trial findings that support the use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and the dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist to reduce CRM risk. We examine key cardiovascular and renal outcomes trials, as well as metabolic-related trials, such as weight loss and the management of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and their alignment with guideline-directed care. In addition to efficacy and safety, we also focus on addressing disparities in access and overcoming implementation challenges, such as low use among specific subpopulations. Lastly, we explore the future of incretin-based therapies, including new triple agonists and ongoing research. Prompt and equitable adoption of GLP-1-based therapeutic options could improve the standard of care for T2D by addressing the entire range of CRM syndrome.

title: Diabesity: an old term, a modern challenge - multi-omics and precision anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in type 2 diabetes.
journal: Journal of pharmacy & pharmaceutical sciences : a publication of the Canadian Society for Pharmaceutical Sciences, Societe canadienne des sciences pharmaceutiques
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity are closely interconnected but heterogeneous conditions in which treatment response, safety, body weight, glycemic control, and long-term clinical outcomes vary substantially between individuals. This narrative review evaluates emerging anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with coexisting T2DM and obesity and examines the translational role of multi-omics in future precision treatment selection. Distinct from reviews focused primarily on obesity pharmacotherapy or omics-based disease stratification, the present review emphasizes the interface between contemporary drug mechanisms, T2DM-associated metabolic heterogeneity, candidate molecular signatures, and the level of evidence required for clinically actionable prescribing. We summarize evidence for approved and investigational oral incretin therapies, dual and triple receptor agonists, amylin-based strategies, established antidiabetic drugs, and adjunctive approaches targeting body composition. Throughout the review, we distinguish established clinical evidence from mechanistic rationale, candidate biomarkers, exploratory associations, and hypothetical future precision applications. We also separate metabolic efficacy endpoints, such as body weight and HbA1c, from intermediate cardiometabolic risk markers and from cardiovascular or kidney outcomes demonstrated in dedicated outcome trials. At present, no genomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, proteomic, microbiome, or integrated multi-omics signature has been clinically validated to select a specific anti-obesity medication for patients with T2DM and obesity. Major unresolved issues include the need for prospective biomarker validation, direct comparative trials, standardized assays, externally validated and calibrated prediction models, preservation of skeletal muscle health and physical function, long-term safety, treatment durability, affordability, and equitable implementation. Multi-omics should therefore be viewed as an investigational framework for generating and testing precision-treatment hypotheses rather than as a basis for routine prescribing.

title: Availability of age-stratified evidence for GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors: an analysis of European public assessment reports with a focus on older patients.
abstract: GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors are widely prescribed and their use is increasingly frequent in older patient populations. We evaluated the extent to which older patients were represented in clinical trials of liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. To identify relevant trials, we screened the respective European Public Assessment Reports (n = 28) and the European Summaries of Product Characteristics (n = 9) for each of the six approved medicines. Further information was retrieved from the original publications of the identified trials and from the ClinicalTrials.gov database (n = 40). Overall, we analyzed n = 185 sources for 106 trial populations. For 46% of the 106 analyzed trial populations, data for patients ≥65 years were identified. Where age distributions were reported, patients aged 75 years or older were markedly underrepresented in nearly all trials, and subgroup analyses of efficacy and safety by age were rarely published. Especially in cardiovascular outcome trials and trials including patients with chronic kidney disease or chronic heart failure, older patients were better represented and analyses of primary outcomes in different age groups were published more frequently. Safety data on different age groups were mainly identified in the European Public Assessment Reports. Whereas increasing numbers of adverse events with older age were observed in several trials, this increase typically affected all trial arms, independent of the drug treatment. Data availability for patients with older age is insufficient from pivotal trials to properly describe efficacy or safety of liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin.

title: Digital Augmentation of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 for Obesity Management: Retrospective Study.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are highly effective for weight management; however, long-term outcomes depend on sustained behavioral engagement. Digital health tools may enhance these behavioral components, but evidence regarding their real-world benefit alongside pharmacotherapy remains limited. This study aims to evaluate whether augmenting a direct-to-consumer GLP-1 RA program with a behavioral support smartphone app improves weight-loss outcomes compared with medication alone, and to identify which app features are associated with weight loss over time. A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted using data from 6113 adults (older than 18 years) in Australia who self-enrolled into the Mosh direct-to-consumer weight-loss program between July 1, 2024, and August 13, 2025, with their weight data recorded at baseline and at least 1 other timepoint. Participants received semaglutide or tirzepatide, with optional access to a smartphone app and clinician support. Logistic regression models examined achievement of ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight-loss thresholds at 60, 120, and 180 days. Linear mixed-effects models interacting with app feature use, with linear and quadratic time terms, assessed the association of different features with percentage weight loss trajectories over time. Both models adjusted for medication type, gender, ethnicity, age, and baseline BMI. Participants using the program plus medication had higher odds of achieving clinically significant weight loss than those using medication only. Adjusted odds ratio point estimates for day 60, 120, and 180 (±10) days indicated they were 1.38 (95% CI 1.09-1.75) times to 2.22 (95% CI 1.40-3.45) times more likely to achieve ≥5% weight loss across timepoints, 1.67 (95% CI 1.33-2.10) times to 1.97 (95% CI 1.35-2.90) times more likely to achieve ≥10% weight loss by day 120 and 180, and 1.99 (95% CI 1.26-3.29) times more likely to achieve ≥15% weight loss by 180 days. Mixed-effects modeling demonstrated that progress logging was associated with more rapid weight loss over time (β=.26 percentage-point additional weight lost per 30 days, SE 0.06; t4336=4.46; 95% CI 0.14-0.38; P<.001). No other app features were consistently associated with changes in weight-loss trajectories. Augmenting GLP-1 RA treatment with a behavioral smartphone app was associated with a higher likelihood of achieving clinically significant weight loss, although differences in overall weight-loss trajectories were modest. Progress logging emerged as the primary behavioral predictor of improved outcomes. While not causal effects, these findings are consistent with the positive value of integrating digital tools with pharmacotherapy for weight loss.

title: From Lifestyle Advice to GLP-1 Agonists: The Transformation of Pediatric Obesity Care.
abstract: Pediatric obesity now affects nearly 1 in 5 children and adolescents in the United States, and its consequences reach well into adult life. For years, clinicians offered little beyond brief advice and a plan to recheck later, an approach that quietly allowed a treatable disease to progress. The 2023 American Academy of Pediatrics guideline broke with that tradition. It treats obesity as a chronic disease and calls for early, intensive treatment that may include medication from age 12 years and metabolic and bariatric surgery from age 13 years. This narrative review summarizes what the authors know about the epidemiology, biology, assessment, and management of pediatric obesity, with a focus on the rapidly changing place of drug therapy. Four medications carry US Food and Drug Administration approval for adolescents: orlistat, phentermine/topiramate extended-release, liraglutide, and once-weekly semaglutide. Of these, semaglutide has shown the greatest effect in randomized trials to date, lowering body mass index by roughly 16% in the STEP TEENS study. Intensive lifestyle treatment remains the foundation at every age, and surgery offers benefit for adolescents with severe obesity. Optimal care also means addressing weight stigma and the social conditions that concentrate risk in disadvantaged communities. The hardest problem now is access: the treatments exist, but they reach children unevenly. Tirzepatide and other newer agents are likely to broaden the options in the near future.

title: Patient-centred outcomes with incretin-based therapies and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a programme-level systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is characterised by symptom burden, impaired mobility, and reduced health status. Direct comparative evidence between incretin-based therapies and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors is lacking. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review and programme-level meta-analysis, using the independent parent randomised trial programme as the unit of analysis to avoid double-counting linked reports. The primary endpoint was the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score, and the secondary endpoint was the six-minute walk distance. Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation with Knapp-Hartung inference. Six parent programmes were included: STEP-heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, STEP-heart failure with preserved ejection fraction DM, SUMMIT, PRESERVED-HF, EMPEROR-Preserved, and DELIVER. In obesity-focused incretin programmes, pooled mean differences were 7.38 Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score points (95% confidence interval, 6.29 to 8.48; I2 = 0.00%) and 17.60 m for six-minute walk distance (95% confidence interval, 10.69 to 24.52; I2 = 0.00%). The secondary sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score synthesis showed a pooled mean difference of 2.53 points (95% confidence interval, −1.97 to 7.03; I2 = 82.21%). No parent programme was judged to be at high risk of bias. Incretin-based therapies showed consistent patient-centred improvements in obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, whereas sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor evidence was derived from broader heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction/heart failure with preserved ejection fraction populations and was more heterogeneous. Cross-class comparisons remain exploratory because of population differences, follow-up differences, limited six-minute walk distance availability, and the absence of direct comparative trials; these findings do not establish class superiority.

title: Oil chain length modulates the microscopic interfacial digestion and physiological feedback of oil in water emulsions.
abstract: The influence of oil chain length (CL) on the microscopic interfacial digestion and physiological feedback of emulsions remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of dispersed phase CL on the digestion of myofibrillar protein (MP) emulsions using an in vivo mouse model and in vitro techniques, specifically the pendant drop-continuous phase replacement method and quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation (QCM-D). Results revealed that LCT formed a denser, more rigid interfacial network, restricting pepsin accessibility and yielding significantly lower gastric protein digestibility at 1 h (66.04 ± 0.93%) than MCT (84.90 ± 0.76%) (p < 0.05). In the intestinal phase, the LCT interface exhibited delayed bile-salt displacement and localized product accumulation, restricting total free fatty acid (FFA) release to 23.49 ± 2.21%, whereas MCT mitigated steric hindrance and product inhibition, driving FFA release to 53.38 ± 1.48%. In vivo, LCT-derived long-chain fatty acids strongly stimulated satiety hormones at 2 h (GLP-1: 27.05 ± 1.34 pg/mL; CCK: 188.42 ± 6.45 pg/mg protein; PYY: 1398.24 ± 72.15 pg/mg protein), triggering duodenal-gastric feedback that delayed gastric emptying and enabled sustained plasma amino acid absorption. Conversely, MCT was rapidly emptied from the stomach and triggered higher plasma amino-acid concentrations at 0.5 h (5.01 ± 0.12 μmol/mL), with its metabolites absorbed directly through the portal vein. Blending LCT and MCT balanced rapid lipolysis with sustained nutrient availability. These results suggest that oil CL regulates interfacial film strength and enzymatic accessibility, thereby modulating nutrient release kinetics, gastric emptying rates, and in vivo endocrine homeostasis.

title: Lifestyle Modification and Bariatric Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes Remission : Short title: Diabetes Remission Strategies in T2DM.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) has traditionally been regarded as a chronic and progressively worsening disease. This paradigm is now challenged by evidence showing that remission is achievable in selected patients, particularly when interventions produce substantial and sustained weight loss. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on lifestyle modification and bariatric/metabolic surgery as remission-inducing strategies, with emphasis on mechanisms, comparative efficacy, predictors of response, and limitations. Intensive lifestyle interventions, especially very-low-calorie diets and total diet replacement programs, can induce normoglycemia in selected individuals through reductions in hepatic and pancreatic fat, improved insulin sensitivity, and partial recovery of β-cell function. However, durability is limited and depends strongly on sustained weight loss. Bariatric/metabolic surgery, particularly Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, achieves higher and more durable remission rates than non-surgical approaches. These effects are mediated by both weight loss and weight-independent mechanisms, including enhanced incretin signaling, altered bile acid metabolism, and gut microbiota changes. Consistent predictors of remission include shorter diabetes duration, lower baseline HbA1c, reduced treatment burden, greater weight loss, and preserved β-cell function. Despite these advances, relapse remains common, long-term randomized data are limited, and important barriers persist, including procedural risk, cost, and inequitable access. Overall, the evidence supports a shift from a model of inevitable progression toward one of potentially reversible metabolic dysfunction, with important implications for early, remission-oriented care.

title: From metabolic therapy to addiction care: a clinical pharmacology roadmap for GLP-1 receptor agonists in substance use disorders.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), established treatments for type 2 diabetes and obesity, are being investigated for substance use disorders (SUDs). Randomized evidence is emerging in alcohol use disorder (AUD), while evidence for opioid, nicotine, cocaine, cannabis, and stimulant use disorders remains mixed, observational, or investigational. This targeted narrative review integrates PubMed/MEDLINE literature, US Food and Drug Administration guidance and labeling, and ClinicalTrials.gov records available through 15 July 2026, with targeted literature and registry updates through 20 October 2026. It evaluates mechanistic plausibility, randomized and real-world human evidence, agent- and dose-specific pharmacology, co-treatment with established SUD medications, safety, adherence, benefit-risk assessment, harm reduction, equity, and trial design. The evidence is sufficient to justify indication-specific clinical development, especially for AUD, but currently insufficient for routine off-label treatment of SUDs for patients without an approved metabolic indication. Near-term research should test GLP-1 RAs as adjuncts rather than replacements for established SUD care, distinguish direct reward effects from weight loss and adverse-effect pathways, and embed risk minimization, patient-important outcomes, and equitable access into development from the outset.

title: Early Treatment Trajectory and Long-Term Persistence to Semaglutide for Obesity: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
abstract: To assess semaglutide persistence in obesity management, identify factors associated with discontinuation and examine early tirzepatide adoption. This retrospective cohort study used Clalit Health Services records of adults without diabetes initiating Wegovy between January and May 2025. Discontinuation was defined as a gap exceeding 60 days after medication coverage ended. Multivariable Cox models, including a Day-90 landmark analysis, assessed discontinuation. Tirzepatide adoption was evaluated following its December 2025 coverage introduction. Among 34 309 participants (67.0% women; mean age 44.6 years), cumulative discontinuation reached 36.5% at 180 days and 67.6% at 365 days. Arab population sector (hazard ratio [HR] 1.65, 95% CI 1.59-1.72), low socioeconomic status (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.17) and current smoking (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.17) were associated with discontinuation. In the day-90 landmark cohort (n = 28 218), remaining on 0.25 versus 1.0 mg was associated with subsequent discontinuation (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.72-2.06), substantially attenuated after adjustment for early refill adherence. Each percentage-point smaller BMI reduction was associated with 3% higher discontinuation hazard (HR 1.03, 95% CI 1.03-1.04). Following tirzepatide availability, 2908 of 33 936 eligible participants (8.6%) initiated treatment over a median 3.1-month observation period. Adoption was associated with higher socioeconomic status and baseline BMI. Semaglutide discontinuation was common and associated with sociodemographic and early treatment characteristics. Day-90 dose and early weight-loss response may help identify discontinuation risk. Socioeconomic differences suggest inequalities in sustained obesity pharmacotherapy access.

title: Research progress on bowel preparation regimens before colonoscopy: a narrative review.
abstract: Adequate bowel preparation is the single most important determinant of colonoscopy quality, yet suboptimal preparation affects up to one-quarter of colonoscopies, leading to repeat procedures, increased health-system costs, and health disparities. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence on bowel preparation regimens through a public health lens, organized around four interconnected dimensions: cleansing efficacy, safety, tolerability, and population-specific applicability. We define and classify preparation regimens by volume (high-volume ≥4 L, low-volume 2-<4 L, ultra-low-volume <2 L) and administration schedule (split-dose, same-day). Low-volume, split-dose formulations achieve non-inferior cleansing efficacy to high-volume 4L polyethylene glycol (PEG) regimens, with improved patient tolerability and compliance. The Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) is the most widely adopted assessment instrument; commonly used adequate preparation is defined as total BBPS ≥6 with each segment ≥2, although definitions vary across studies. PEG-based preparations maintain the most favorable safety profile, particularly in patients with renal or cardiovascular comorbidities, while sodium phosphate carries a small but clinically significant risk of acute phosphate nephropathy. Special populations-including older adults with frailty and polypharmacy, patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and those with diabetes-require tailored preparation strategies. Emerging evidence on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), linaclotide, simethicone, dietary optimization, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based bowel preparation assessment is critically evaluated. Health system implications, including the impact of inadequate preparation on resource utilization, adherence barriers linked to health literacy, and equity considerations, are examined. The review concludes that no single regimen is universally optimal; personalized preparation strategies integrating risk stratification, AI-assisted quality assessment, and evidence-based adjunctive protocols represent the most promising path toward improving colonoscopy outcomes at the population level.

title: Prescription denials for GLP-1 receptor agonists across commercial, Medicare, and Medicaid coverage, 2018-2024.
abstract: Access to GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) remains strongly shaped by payer coverage and utilization management. Patient-level evidence on GLP-1 RA denial across payer types is limited. Using a national multi-payer claims database capturing adjudication status of pharmacy claims, we examined GLP-1 RA prescription denial and whether individuals with an index denial subsequently obtained a paid fill from 2018 to 2024. The index claim was defined as each individual's first observed GLP-1 RA claim. We estimated multivariable logistic regressions to examine factors associated with index-claim denial and the likelihood of receiving a paid fill within 90 days among individuals with a denied index claim. Overall, 7.9% of individuals had a denied index GLP-1 RA claim, increasing from 4.0% (2018) to 9.6% (2022) before declining to 6.6% (2024). Denial was higher in Medicaid than in commercial coverage (12.6% vs 5.6%) and for obesity-indicated than diabetes-indicated brands (16.8% vs 6.3%). Among individuals with a denied index claim, 34.1% obtained a paid fill within 90 days, declining from 45.9% (2018) to 24.8% (2024). Denial was concentrated in Medicaid and obesity-indicated products, and most individuals with a denied index claim did not obtain a paid fill within 90 days.

title: Combined melatonin and edaravone therapy attenuates methylmercury-induced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like neurodegeneration through GLP-1 modulation and myelin preservation.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, resulting in progressive muscle weakness, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Despite the availability of disease-modifying therapies, current treatment options provide only modest clinical benefits, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting multiple pathological mechanisms. Melatonin, a pleiotropic neuroprotective molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, has emerged as a promising candidate; however, its influence on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-associated neuroprotective signaling and related molecular events in ALS remains poorly understood. Therefore, the present study investigated the neuroprotective efficacy of melatonin in a methylmercury (MTMR)-induced rat model of ALS and explored its effects on GLP-1-associated molecular alterations, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, demyelination, and neuronal injury. Molecular docking analysis was performed to predict the interaction of melatonin with proteins implicated in ALS pathology. Adult Wistar rats were exposed to MTMR (5 mg/kg, p.o.) for 21 days to induce ALS-like neurodegeneration, followed by treatment with melatonin (5 or 10 mg/kg, i.p.), edaravone (3 mg/kg, i.p.), or their combination for an additional 21 days. Neurobehavioral performance, biochemical alterations, hematological parameters, molecular biomarkers, and histopathological changes were subsequently evaluated. MTMR administration produced profound motor deficits accompanied by reduced GLP-1 levels, neurotransmitter imbalance, increased neuroinflammatory and apoptotic markers, elevated neurofilament light chain (NEFL), skeletal muscle injury, methylmercury accumulation, and extensive myelin and neuronal damage. Melatonin treatment significantly attenuated these pathological alterations in a dose-dependent manner by increasing GLP-1 levels, improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory and apoptotic responses, restoring neurotransmitter balance, preserving myelin integrity, and improving neuronal morphology across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord. Molecular docking further predicted favorable interactions between melatonin and several proteins associated with ALS pathophysiology, supporting its potential as a multitarget therapeutic agent. In most outcome measures, combined treatment with melatonin and edaravone produced greater neuroprotective effects than either intervention alone. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that melatonin substantially attenuates methylmercury-induced ALS-like neuropathology through coordinated modulation of multiple pathological processes associated with neurodegeneration. Although the precise molecular mechanisms require further experimental validation, the observed restoration of GLP-1 levels together with improvements in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, and myelin integrity suggests that melatonin may represent a promising adjunctive therapeutic strategy for ALS.

title: Pediatric obesity pharmacotherapy: a practical guide for general pediatricians.
abstract: Multimodal treatment approaches to pediatric obesity, including pharmacotherapy, are now recommended as part of an early intervention strategy to improve long-term health outcomes. However, barriers to prescribing obesity medications limit patient access to them. This review summarizes practical approaches to pediatric obesity pharmacotherapy tailored for the general pediatrician, based on evidence and expert opinion. The American Academy of Pediatrics clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of pediatric obesity calls for early, individualized intervention, including consideration of pharmacotherapy. Available obesity medications include those that are Federal Drug Administration (FDA)-approved for this indication and those that are used "off-label" with FDA approval for other indications. Obesity pharmacotherapy should be considered an adjunct to lifestyle interventions for pediatric obesity. Readiness to prescribe these medications is influenced by physician comfort, practice infrastructure, and access-related barriers. Specialty training (i.e., endocrinology, gastroenterology, obesity medicine) does not have to be a requirement for managing obesity.

title: The Role of Milk and Dairy Products in Type 2 Diabetes and Prediabetes: A Narrative Review of Randomized Trials.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The influence of milk and dairy products on glucose metabolism, prediabetes and type 2 diabetes is controversial. The topic has taken on new relevance following the release of the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines For Americans, recommending full-fat dairy with no added sugars on a daily basis. The purpose of this narrative review is to summarize evidence from randomized trials on the potential effects of milk and dairy products on glycemic parameters. Methods: For this narrative review we conducted a PubMed literature search for randomized controlled trials with combined search terms (dairy AND diabetes mellitus type 2) OR (dairy products AND diabetes mellitus type 2) OR (dairy AND pre diabetes) OR (dairy products AND pre diabetes). Eligible trials enrolled adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes and analyzed the influence of a milk or dairy-product intervention on glycemic markers. Included trials had full text availability and were published in English or German. Results: After screening for inclusion criteria, we identified 46 studies for type 2 diabetes and 11 trials for prediabetes. Findings of included studies are presented categorized by type 2 diabetes and prediabetes cohorts, by dairy intervention and by effects on acute (e.g., postprandial glucose, insulin and incretin concentrations) and chronic (e.g., hemoglobin A1c, fructosamine) glycemic control. Conclusions: Dairy products require a differentiated view, as their glycemic effects in people with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes vary substantially by dairy matrix, dose, timing, and specific fortification.

title: Progress in Anti-Obesity Drug Development: A Pharmacodynamics Perspective.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Obesity is a chronic, multifactorial condition driven by complex neuroendocrine and metabolic pathways that limit the long-term success of lifestyle interventions. Pharmacotherapy has advanced from early monoaminergic agents to incretin-based and multi-receptor agonists with substantially improved efficacy. This review aims to provide pharmacodynamics-focused synthesis of current and emerging anti-obesity medications, emphasizing mechanistic targets, receptor interactions, and translational implications. Methods: We conducted a narrative review integrating Phase I-III clinical trials, mechanistic pharmacology data (receptor affinity, potency, and signaling bias), and regulatory summaries for FDA-approved and selected emerging, investigational, repurposed, or regionally approved anti-obesity agents. Inclusion focused on clinical relevance, pharmacodynamic novelty, and weight-loss efficacy. Results: Approved anti-obesity medications act through diverse pathways, including the inhibition of fat absorption (orlistat), the modulation of central appetite circuits (phentermine/topiramate, naltrexone/bupropion), and incretin-based mechanisms (liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, and the oral GLP-1 receptor agonists semaglutide 25 mg and the nonpeptide orforglipron). GLP-1 receptor agonists achieve approximately 6-15% weight loss, while dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists such as tirzepatide reach 15-20%. Emerging agents-including triple agonists (retatrutide), glucagon-based co-agonists, amylin analogs with Phase III efficacy data, earlier-stage growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) pathway agonists, and peripherally restricted cannabinoid-1 receptor inverse agonists-demonstrate enhanced metabolic effects and potential improvements in lean-mass preservation. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics highlight the need for individualized dosing strategies. Conclusions: Clinical efficacy and tolerability cannot be inferred from receptor identity alone. They emerge from relative receptor potency and efficacy, exposure, tissue access, receptor trafficking, and mechanism-linked adverse effects. Dual and triple agonists can broaden efficacy, but receptor balance and standardized comparative pharmacology remain essential for rational development and individualized dosing.

title: Do Gastric Balloons Have a Future? Intragastric Balloons in the Era of Highly Effective Obesity Pharmacotherapy.
abstract: Intragastric balloons (IGBs) were developed to bridge the gap between lifestyle intervention and Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (MBS), but the advent of highly efficacious pharmacotherapies and Endoscopic Sleeve Gastroplasty (ESG) has challenged their role. This narrative review synthesises contemporary evidence and guideline recommendations regarding IGBs, focusing on short-term efficacy, durability, safety, psychological aspects, and health system considerations in comparison with Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1 RAs), dual GIP (Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide)/GLP-1 RAs, ESG, and MBS. Across randomised trials and meta-analyses, IGBs consistently produce modest short-term weight loss of approximately 10-15% total body weight at six months, with frequent weight regain following removal and limited long-term benefit. In contrast, modern pharmacotherapy achieves greater and more durable weight loss with fewer procedural risks. Current guidelines therefore position IGBs as adjunctive or bridging interventions reserved for selected patient subgroups, rather than as a dominant intermediate therapy. Overall, current evidence supports a selective role for IGBs as bridging, adjunctive, or combination interventions within multimodal obesity pathways, particularly for patients who cannot access or tolerate pharmacotherapy or who require a behavioural and metabolic bridge to surgery.

title: GLP-1-Based Therapies for Cardiovascular Risk Reduction in Kazakhstan: Evidence, Affordability, Equity and Implementation Considerations.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide and is the principal cause of death in low- and middle-income countries. Although cardiovascular outcome trials have established the benefits of Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) in reducing major adverse cardiovascular events, the translation of this evidence into routine clinical practice in Central Asia remains limited and underexplored. Specifically, in Kazakhstan, despite measurable improvements in cardiac infrastructure over the past decade, critical gaps persist in early diagnosis, cardiometabolic risk stratification, and the integration of newer pharmacological strategies into routine practice. In this review, we aim to evaluate the potential role of GLP-1-based therapies within the current cardiovascular prevention landscape in Kazakhstan. It also synthesizes current mechanistic evidence and findings from major clinical trials supporting the use of GLP-1RAs as cardiometabolic agents with potential cardiovascular benefits. Furthermore, we examine the practical factors that may influence their adoption within Kazakhstan's health system, including accessibility, affordability, clinician preparedness, prescribing capacity, regulatory considerations, and policy integration. By integrating evidence from cardiovascular outcome trials, clinical studies, and health-system perspectives, this review seeks to provide a balanced assessment of the potential contribution of GLP-1-based therapies to cardiovascular risk reduction in Kazakhstan while identifying priorities for future research, implementation strategies, and health policy development.

title: Post-Initiation Care Patterns and Weight Loss With Semaglutide and Tirzepatide for Obesity in Clinical Practice.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Randomized trials show substantial weight loss with semaglutide and tirzepatide under structured care, but little is known about whether patients in routine practice continue therapy, reach a maintenance dose, and have their weight measured. To describe the first year after initiation of semaglutide or tirzepatide for obesity, including care patterns, maintenance-dose attainment, weight documentation, and total body weight loss (TBWL). This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos, an electronic health record network of >350 US health systems, to identify adults with obesity and without diabetes who initiated injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide in 2024. Outcomes over 12 months included prescribing persistence, discontinuation, switching, add-on therapy, and reinitiation; attainment of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-labeled maintenance doses; availability of follow-up weight; and TBWL across progressively restricted populations. Among 743,153 adults (60.1% semaglutide; mean age, 48.5 years; 72.5% female), 12-month prescribing persistence was 29.9% for semaglutide and 35.9% for tirzepatide. FDA-labeled maintenance-dose attainment was 28.3% and 55.0%, respectively, and only 8.8% and 16.4% remained prescribing persistent at a maintenance dose with a recorded weight at 12 months. About half of initiators lacked a 12-month weight. Among all initiators, ≥5% TBWL was documented in 25.6% (semaglutide) and 30.4% (tirzepatide), rising to 51.9% and 61.9% among those with recorded weight, 66.1% and 79.5% among those also prescribing persistent, and 82.9% and 87.3% among those further at a maintenance dose. In routine practice, most patients initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide did not remain on therapy, reach a maintenance dose, and have weight documented through the first year. Documented weight loss was greatest among those completing each step of care, suggesting continuation, dose escalation, and monitoring as targets for improvement. Care Cascade and Weight-Loss Outcomes Among Semaglutide and Tirzepatide Initiators, Standardized to 100 Initiators.Numbers are per 100 initiators and were rounded so that categories at each step sum to the preceding step. At the 12-month dose step, prescribed dose was missing for 1 per 100 semaglutide initiators and <1 per 100 tirzepatide initiators.

title: Pharmacotherapy for MASLD: current evidence and challenges in clinical practice.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is characterized by a complex pathophysiology driven by intertwined metabolic and hepatic pathways, enabling the identification of multiple therapeutic targets and a rapidly expanding drug development pipeline. This review summarizes the current and emerging therapeutic landscape for MASLD and discusses key challenges for clinical implementation. The imminent availability of several new therapies is expected to pose important clinical challenges, particularly in accurately identifying patients most likely to benefit. Currently, resmetirom and semaglutide are the only two drugs conditionally approved for patients with fibrosis stages 2-3, pending final phase 3 outcomes, and represent the main liver-directed and metabolic-focused therapeutic strategies, respectively. Treatment selection should follow a phenotype-based approach integrating metabolic profile and liver disease stage. Non-invasive tests are central for assessing treatment eligibility; however, strategies incorporating metabolic risk profiling and longitudinal monitoring will be essential to optimize real-world management of MASH.

title: The Veterans Affairs Pentoxifylline in Diabetic Kidney Disease (VA PTXRx) Study: Baseline Characteristics.
journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
abstract: Experimental and clinical data suggest that the non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor pentoxifylline (PTX) reduces proteinuria and may delay the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). However, no large-scale randomized clinical trial has determined whether PTX can reduce end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and mortality in DKD. VA PTXRx is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter clinical trial designed to test the hypothesis that PTX, when added to usual care, prolongs the time to kidney failure or death in type 2 diabetic (T2D) participants with DKD compared to usual care plus placebo. Enrolled participants at very high risk for ESKD and/or death were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either PTX 400 mg twice daily or matching placebo using randomly permuted blocks with stratification for site, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (RAAS) inhibitor use, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage. The study is event-driven, requiring 646 primary events (ESKD (chronic dialysis or transplantation) or death) to achieve 80% power to detect a relative risk reduction of 19% with PTX. Between December 2019 and November 2025, 2376 participants at 34 VA sites in the USA were randomized. The mean age at randomization was 72.3 years (SD 7.7), with 97% being male. The mean baseline eGFR was 33.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 (SD 9.4). The median urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) was 401 mg/g (IQR 122-1076). At baseline, the usage of RAAS inhibitors was 80.0%, sodium-glucose transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors 52.9%, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists 33.2%, and finerenone 3.0%. The majority (88%) of participants had stage 3B or 4 CKD (eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73m2). The results, anticipated in 2027, are expected to determine whether PTX is a treatment option for patients with high-risk DKD. Because PTX is a generic medication, it is inexpensive in many health systems, which would facilitate access if it proves effective. Trial Registration: This study is registered with clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT03625648).

title: Acarbose differentially affects gut microbial metabolism of maltose and sucrose, distinctly modulating host metabolism.
abstract: Gut microbiota act as beneficial symbionts of the hosts. Administration of α-glucosidase inhibitors (α-GIs) is considered to promote the microbiota's carbohydrate availability, modulating short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. However, it remains unclear whether host-microbiota interaction differs depending on α-GI types (e.g., acarbose versus miglitol) and carbohydrate types co-administered. In this study, we demonstrate that acarbose is transported through bacterial outer membrane porins, LamB and ScrY, and inhibits maltose metabolism in Escherichia coli. Furthermore, studies using Klebsiella pneumoniae reveal that acarbose suppresses utilization of maltose, but not that of sucrose. When co-administered with acarbose in mice, sucrose, relative to maltose, enhances SCFA production, suppresses glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) secretion, and protects against high-fat diet-induced obesity, underscoring the importance of sucrose as a microbiota-dependent beneficial factor, but not a culprit in host metabolism. In conclusion, acarbose regulates host metabolic processes partly by modulating gut microbial metabolism in a carbohydrate-type-dependent manner.

title: Global insulin supply insecurity and the role of manufacturing innovation.
abstract: Insulin availability and affordability have long limited access in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and recent shortages and product withdrawals in higher-income settings underscore the need for reliable supply worldwide. While documented disruptions do not establish an aggregate global manufacturing deficit, commercial decisions, regulatory barriers, procurement, financing, and distribution can restrict access even where production capacity exists. Nevertheless, product prioritization and investment decisions can constrain the capacity allocated to insulin and reduce the ability to respond to changing demand. This narrative review examines global insulin demand, supply insecurity, market structure, affordability, and health-system barriers, distinguishing the circumstances of the United States, other high-income countries, and LMICs. We consider the potential effects of incretin therapies on insulin requirements and industrial investment and assess manufacturing modernization, including continuous production, as one component of a broader response. Proposed technological benefits require insulin-specific validation of quality, productivity, cost, and commercial feasibility. Priorities include stronger shortage surveillance, diversified qualified suppliers, regulatory cooperation, sustainable procurement, reduced waste, and dependable distribution. Supply security must extend through safe storage, administration, education, and glucose monitoring. Coordinated action across manufacturing and health systems is needed to maintain uninterrupted, affordable access to appropriate insulin treatment.

title: Prevention Before Therapy in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: The Clinical, Economic, and Human Case for Weighting Resources Upstream.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is projected to become the second-leading cause of US cancer death by 2030, and survival is dominated by stage at diagnosis: roughly 44% at five years for localized disease versus about 3% with distant metastases. Only about 15% of cases are detected while localized, surgery reaches a minority of patients, and no validated screening test exists for average-risk adults. This topical review examines the biologic, clinical, economic, psychological, equity, and therapeutic evidence bearing on where scarce resources should be directed. The long interval between initiating mutation and invasive disease provides a mechanistic rationale for prevention and interception, and the modifiable exposures of obesity, tobacco, type 2 diabetes, and alcohol act largely within that window. We consider innovations that extend prevention beyond lifestyle advice-incretin-based weight management, risk stratification anchored in new-onset diabetes and biomarkers, and immunoprevention-together with early-onset disease, implementation and policy, and the barriers and evidentiary limits that temper these arguments. We propose a three-tier framework of primary prevention, early detection in high-risk groups, and therapy, and argue that research, policy, and clinical investment should be weighted upstream, because every case prevented spares the cost, capacity, and suffering that the downstream tiers must otherwise absorb.

title: Obesity: oral therapy for those afraid of needles.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) pharmacotherapy has transformed obesity management, yet subcutaneous administration remains a barrier for patients with needle phobia. This review examines needle phobia and agoraphobia as contributors to treatment non-adherence and evaluates the evidence for oral GLP-1 RA alternatives. We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology of needle phobia (trypanophobia) and agoraphobia, their mechanisms and psychiatric comorbidities, real-world discontinuation rates of injectable GLP-1 RAs, and clinical efficacy data for oral semaglutide and emerging oral agents. A brief overview of the literature search methodology (PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov; searched to June 2026) is provided in the Introduction. A structured clinical decision algorithm is proposed. Oral semaglutide 25 mg/day (the currently approved dose for weight management) demonstrates weight loss of similar magnitude to subcutaneous formulations across separate trials and should be considered preferentially in patients with moderate-to-severe needle phobia. Systematic needle phobia screening at obesity clinic entry, combined with a severity-based treatment algorithm integrating pharmacological and psychological approaches, is recommended to maximize equitable access to obesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Health Policy for Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome in Asian Health Systems: Three Design Principles, Three Binding Constraints, and the Governance That Decides between Them.
abstract: Obesity drives metabolic syndrome and cardiometabolic disease in Asia, where complications develop at lower levels of adiposity than in Western populations. We reviewed Asian obesity policies to identify design features that support their durability and how access to incretin-based medications fits within these policies. This narrative review used a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase (January 2000 to March 2025) supplemented by grey literature from public health agencies. Of 1,884 records, 612 underwent full-text review and 236 met inclusion criteria. Two reviewers screened independently, resolving disagreements by consensus. Evidence was grouped into healthcare-based prevention and treatment, fiscal and regulatory measures, food and physical activity environments, digital health, and pharmacotherapy access. We examined Japan's Specific Health Checkup, Korea's National Health Screening Program, Singapore's Nutri-Grade scheme, and sugar-sweetened beverage taxes in Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines. Three design principles emerged: holding insurers accountable for population metabolic screening, scheduling excise tax increases in advance, and adapting regulation to local food settings, including freshly prepared foods. Their effectiveness was limited by stigma in workplace screening, limited reach into the informal food sector, and lower uptake in rural and digitally underserved populations. Policy durability depended more on governance than on individual measures. Obesity policy in Asia requires governance mechanisms built into its design: a permanent inter-agency body with protected funding, legal safeguards against industry interference, and mandatory equity audits with independent monitoring. Access to incretin-based medications belongs in the same framework; otherwise, these drugs may widen regional inequities.

title: Liraglutide Dose Affordability and Durability in Real-World Obesity Care.
Semaglutide in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction and Obesity: The Gap Between Discussion and Use.
abstract: Semaglutide improves symptoms and physical function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and obesity. Whether discussion of treatment is accompanied by its use in routine care is less well understood. We retrospectively assessed treatment discussion, follow-up medication records and documented reasons for non-initiation in 159 patients from a prospective registry. Available follow-up information was retained when assessment dates were incompletely transcribed. Associations with registry-recorded diabetes or prediabetes were explored using Firth logistic regression. Semaglutide was discussed or offered in 148/159 patients (93.1%). Among 148 baseline nonusers with subsequent medication information, it was newly recorded in 23 (15.5%). Recorded diabetes or prediabetes was associated with this outcome (adjusted odds ratio 3.76, 95% confidence interval 1.08-19.93), but a sensitivity analysis restricting the reference group by glycated haemoglobin was inconclusive. Among 125 patients without subsequently recorded semaglutide, affordability concerns were documented in 55 (44.0%), safety concerns in 48 (38.4%), and both in 38 (30.4%). Frequent discussion of semaglutide coexisted with infrequent documentation of subsequent use. Financial and medication-related concerns commonly overlapped. These findings identify a gap in routine care without establishing its causal determinants or verifying treatment initiation.

title: The effects of improved access to diabetes medications on risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: Diabetes is associated with elevated risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Disease management with pharmaceutical therapies may mitigate this increased risk, but access and use of diabetes therapies are limited, especially for persons at highest risk of ADRD. Using 10 years of data on Americans aged 51 and older with diabetes, we employed dynamic microsimulation to analyze the impact of increased utilization of glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP1s) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2s) on ADRD incidence. Over 10 years, utilization of GLP1s and SGLT2s by people with diabetes and HbA1c > 7 could avert 76,000-201,000 ADRD cases. The risk reduction is largest for Black and Hispanic individuals and individuals with HbA1c > 8. This study shows that improving diabetes management can lead to large reductions in ADRD risk. Improved adherence and access for those with higher HbA1c and higher risk of ADRD will have the largest benefit.

title: Hope, hype, and high costs: Navigating glucagon-like Peptide-1 based therapy initiation among young adults.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies have emerged as a major option for weight management, with prescribing among young adults increasing nearly sixfold between 2020 and 2023 in the United States. Despite this growth, little is known about how young adults decide to initiate GLP-1 therapy, navigate access, and manage treatment costs. This study examined individual, social, financial, and structural influences shaping GLP-1 initiation for weight management among young adults. This was a qualitative interview study that employed a semi-structured interview design utilizing a hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis framework guided by Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use. We recruited 25 young adults aged 18-30 years from the South Florida community who were currently using or had used GLP-1-based therapy for weight management within the preceding 12 months. Transcripts were coded deductively based on constructs from Andersen's model and inductively from themes identified directly from participant narratives. Participants had a mean age of 22 years; 20 (80%) were female and 19 (76%) identified as Hispanic or Latino. Four themes were identified: (1) motivations and expectations for initiation, including health needs, appearance-related goals, and social media-shaped expectations; (2) social and clinical pathways to GLP-1 introduction, particularly family networks and social media; (3) navigation of access pathways ranging from conventional clinical care to medical spas, telehealth, and unregulated self-procurement; and (4) financial barriers characterized by out-of-pocket costs and insurance exclusions that contributed to informal procurement. Within this sample, GLP-1 initiation among young adults was shaped by intersecting health needs, social influences, access structures, and financial constraints rather than by clinical considerations alone. Findings highlight that healthcare systems, policymakers, and public health practitioners must prioritize clinically appropriate access, reliable medication sourcing, and consistent clinical oversight to promote equity and safety among young adults.

title: Tirzepatide persistence, adherence, and dose escalation in a real-world setting with high out-of-pocket costs: a Polish cohort study.
abstract: Tirzepatide is effective in clinical trials, but its real-world use where obesity pharmacotherapy is self-funded remains poorly characterized. We aimed to characterize tirzepatide persistence, adherence, and dose escalation in a high out-of-pocket-cost setting. We retrospectively analyzed nationwide electronic health records from a large Polish private healthcare provider. We included 3030 adults with a first recorded tirzepatide prescription between November 2023 and February 2025. The primary endpoint was time to observed treatment discontinuation. Multivariable Cox regression identified persistence predictors, while adherence was assessed using proportion of days covered (PDC). Successful titration was escalation from 2.5 or 5 mg to ≥10 mg. The cohort included 69.0% women; 83.3% had obesity and 20.0% had type 2 diabetes. Higher first recorded dose was associated with earlier loss of observed treatment. Compared with 2.5 mg initiators, the hazard ratio for discontinuation was 1.44 (95%CI 1.26-1.64, p < 0.001) for 15 mg and 1.24 (95%CI 1.12-1.39, p < 0.001) for 10 mg doses. Traditional comorbidities did not independently predict persistence (all p > 0.10). Among385 patients persistent for ≥180 days, median PDC was 0.86 (IQR 0.73-0.95), with 68% classified as adherent (PDC ≥80%). Of 2194 eligible low-dose patients, 565 (25.8%) escalated to ≥10 mg, corresponding to 18.6% of the full cohort. Real-world tirzepatide persistence was suboptimal and associated with recorded starting dose. Traditional clinical comorbidities had limited impact on discontinuation timing. Nonclinical factors, including affordability, tolerability, and patient expectations, may contribute to early loss of observed treatment; although these were not directly measured.

title: A stewardship framework for incretin-based therapies in weight management.
journal: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA
abstract: Use of incretin-based therapies, including GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists, for weight management and related cardio-kidney-liver-metabolic comorbidities has expanded rapidly, yet real-world practice is challenged by inconsistent prescribing, access barriers, limited long-term safety data, low treatment persistence, and concerns regarding equity and financial sustainability. These gaps highlight the need for a structured, coordinated stewardship model to guide safe and evidence-based use of incretin-based therapies. To develop a scalable, multidisciplinary stewardship framework for incretin-based therapies that supports consistent and efficient prescribing practices, optimizes patient outcomes, strengthens medication access and safety monitoring, and defines the role of pharmacists in chronic weight management. Two sequential expert workgroups were convened, composed of clinicians and pharmacy leaders from 21 health systems. Workgroup 1 identified foundational stewardship elements drawing from established antimicrobial and opioid stewardship models. Workgroup 2 applied these core principles to incretin-based therapies, informed by real-world challenges, emerging evidence, and clinical experience in weight and diabetes management. Consensus was established using a Delphi process, with ≥60% agreement required for inclusion. Workgroups reached consensus on a stewardship framework comprising multidisciplinary leadership, stakeholder engagement, pharmacy expertise, defined priorities, evidence-based interventions, education, data and reporting strategies, communication pathways, and mechanisms for feedback and continuous assessment. In addition, consensus-based pharmacist-led initiatives and metric categories were developed to support implementation and program evaluation across varied ambulatory environments, with pharmacists identified as central to therapy initiation and titration, adverse effect management, access navigation, patient education, and care coordination. A structured stewardship model offers a feasible and scalable approach to optimize incretin-based therapies in weight management. By integrating multidisciplinary collaboration with pharmacy expertise and clinical and operational strategies, health systems can promote safe, equitable, and sustainable use of these therapies, improve population-level outcomes, and safeguard long-term value amid rapidly expanding utilization.

title: Sociodemographic disparities in semaglutide and tirzepatide prescription for obesity treatment.
abstract: Semaglutide and tirzepatide, the 2 most recently approved glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, have demonstrated substantial effectiveness in weight management. However, evidence on treatment inequities remains limited. This study assesses temporal trends and sociodemographic disparities in semaglutide and tirzepatide prescription. Using claims data from Komodo Health, we identified commercially insured individuals aged 18-64 years with overweight or obesity but without type 2 diabetes. We estimated 6-month cumulative incidence of semaglutide and tirzepatide prescription across sociodemographic groups and examined disparities by health care provider socioeconomic status. Six-month cumulative incidence of prescription increased from 1.9% to 16.6% over the study period. Higher access was associated with being female, non-Hispanic White, in higher body mass index categories, and seen at a higher socioeconomic status (SES)-quartile provider. Uptake was significantly lower in lower provider neighborhood SES groups (lowest quartile adjusted odds ratio: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.73-0.78, compared with the highest quartile), and the differences widened over time. The SES disparities were more pronounced at lower BMI categories. Prescription of semaglutide and tirzepatide increased rapidly from 2021 to 2025. Sociodemographic disparities widened over time. Policies addressing provider-level resourcing and pharmaco-equity in drug benefit design are needed to prevent these therapies from exacerbating existing health disparities.

title: Beyond efficacy: the treatment lifecycle of incretin and multi-receptor agonists.
abstract: Incretin and multi-receptor agonist therapies have delivered the widest range of cardiometabolic benefit of any pharmacological class in a generation, with documented benefit across obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular and renal outcomes, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, obstructive sleep apnea, and metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. A substantial fraction of the cardiovascular benefit is weight independent. The pivotal trial evidence is now mature, extending to the dedicated tirzepatide cardiovascular outcome program. The clinical and system-level processes that govern long-term cardiovascular and metabolic benefit, however, lie largely outside the efficacy envelope that these trials measure. Real-world persistence is approximately one-third at 12 months in non-diabetic obesity. Discontinuation is dominated by cost rather than therapeutic failure. Weight and cardiometabolic gains revert toward baseline within months of abrupt cessation. Cyclical use has emerged as a common real-world pattern among adults who discontinue and then restart therapy. Our review proposes a lifecycle framework that organizes the evidence along the patient journey from initiation through titration, on-treatment trajectory, adverse-event landscape, persistence, discontinuation, and reinitiation. Tirzepatide serves as the analytical center of gravity; the selective GLP-1 receptor agonist literature serves as the mature comparator. Seven analytical positions are advanced, and five specific trial designs are named as the research agenda the field requires, four of which remain unaddressed. The work ahead is to align trials, prescribing pathways, and access systems with the chronic-pharmacotherapy reality of the class.

title: The Conventional Cost-Effectiveness and Distributional Cost-Effectiveness of Semaglutide for Obesity Treatment.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the conventional and distributional cost-effectiveness of semaglutide, laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG), and a "do nothing" option in Black and White racial subgroups. A Markov simulation model was developed from a healthcare perspective over a 25-year time horizon for Black and White adults, aged 65-70, with BMI ≥ 35 and cardiovascular disease. Three interventions were modeled: semaglutide 2.4 mg, LSG, and "do nothing." Semaglutide and LSG interventions are cost-effective compared to a "do nothing" strategy (ICERs = $7300/QALY and $12,100/QALY, respectively). Compared to semaglutide, LSG is more expensive but cost-effective (ICER = $53,700/QALY). Semaglutide is more equitable but is not distributionally cost-effective compared to LSG, because it has a lower EDE within our defined inequality aversion (ε) range. Across 10,000 probabilistic iterations, LSG has a 57% probability and semaglutide has a 43% probability of being the most cost-effective at the willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000/QALY. Semaglutide becomes distributionally cost-effective when ε ≥ 14.72, where equity impacts of semaglutide outweigh the conventional cost-effectiveness outcomes. LSG is the most conventionally cost-effective treatment option with some uncertainty. Semaglutide is marginally more equitable than LSG but is not a distributionally cost-effective strategy.

title: The Future of Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery in the Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Era: Has the Scalpel Become Obsolete?
abstract: Obesity remains a growing global health crisis, affecting nearly one billion adults worldwide and substantially increasing the risk of cardiometabolic disease, malignancy, and premature mortality. Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) has evolved into an effective and durable treatment for severe obesity, providing sustained weight loss and significant remission of obesity-related comorbidities (i.e., type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease). Despite dramatic improvements in safety, efficacy, and long-term outcomes over time, MBS remains markedly underutilized, reaching fewer than 1% of eligible patients. Persistent barriers include limited patient and provider awareness, misconceptions regarding surgical risk, and significant disparities in access to care. Concurrently, the rapid adoption of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) has transformed the medical management of obesity, offering effective pharmacologic weight loss but raising questions regarding their impact on MBS utilization, durability, and cost-effectiveness. Emerging evidence demonstrates that while MBS produces greater and more durable weight loss than GLP-1 RAs alone, these therapies need not be competitive. Rather, GLP-1 RAs may serve as 'neoadjuvant' treatment to optimize surgical candidacy or as adjunctive treatment for inadequate weight loss or postoperative weight regain. This review synthesizes contemporary data on MBS procedures, outcomes, disparities in access, and evolving perceptions of obesity treatment in the GLP-1 RA era. We propose a chronic weight management model that integrates pharmacotherapy, surgery, and multidisciplinary care along a continuous treatment spectrum. Positioning MBS and GLP-1 RAs as complementary modalities within individualized care pathways may improve long-term outcomes, expand access, and better address the complex, chronic nature of obesity.

title: Disparities in GLP-1RA and SGLT2i Uptake: a Systematic Review and an Equity-First Framework for Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Care.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) improve cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic outcomes, but equitable access remains a major challenge. This review synthesizes U.S. evidence on disparities in their use and proposes an Equity-First Framework for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic care to advance pharmacoequity. Across 100 U.S.o studies published from 2013 to 2026, the most consistent inequities involved race and ethnicity, socioeconomic status, insurance coverage, age, and access to specialty care, while geographic and sex-related patterns were more heterogeneous. Black and Hispanic patients, Medicaid beneficiaries, lower-income populations, and older adults frequently experienced lower prescribing or initiation. Although use increased following landmark trials and guideline updates, uptake remained well below the eligible population, and disparities persisted or widened for some newer agents. Barriers spanned societal and policy, health-system, provider, patient, and therapy-related domains. Achieving pharmacoequity will require coordinated, multilevel implementation. Our framework links equity-relevant factors and implementation determinants to actionable strategies, including equity monitoring, identification and engagement of eligible patients, equitable care pathways, reduction of structural access barriers, and support for clinicians and patients.

title: Obesity in CKD: The Double-Edged Sword.
abstract: Obesity and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are converging global epidemics with a complex, bidirectional relationship. Obesity directly drives de novo CKD and accelerates its progression via hemodynamic, metabolic, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine pathways culminating in obesity-related glomerulopathy. While advanced and dialysis-dependent CKD exhibit an "obesity paradox, " where higher BMI correlates with survival, this is largely driven by reverse causality, survival bias, and BMI's failure to capture true body composition. Emerging metrics like the Body Roundness Index (BRI) demonstrate that central adiposity remains harmful in dialysis populations, with no paradox found in early CKD or kidney transplantation, adding a second, under-recognised dimension to this dual burden. Beyond progression, obesity significantly increases technical risks for core procedures: kidney biopsies, vascular access creation, peritoneal catheter insertion, and kidney transplantation. This review translates these procedural risks into practical optimization strategies, establishes that intentional, structured weight loss in obese CKD individuals is not associated with the excess mortality attributed to unintentional weight loss in CKD. An expanded overview of body composition assessment methods, contemporary and emerging pharmacotherapy including dual incretin agonists, and bariatric and metabolic surgery, including its role and timing relative to kidney transplantation, is presented, alongside a research agenda emphasising precision obesity management and artificial intelligence-assisted risk prediction.

title: Tirzepatide and Glucagon-like Peptide-1/Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide Therapy: Quality of Life, Filipino Diet Culture, and Safe Access.
Building the Business Case for Access to Obesity Treatment.
The Changing Landscape of Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery: Aligning Access With the Clinical Obesity Framework.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) is the most effective treatment for severe obesity, yet it remains profoundly underutilized. Patients seeking MBS face pretreatment requirements, including mandatory psychological evaluation, documented failed diet attempts, and months of lifestyle interventions that are substantially more extensive than those required for most common gastrointestinal procedures. These requirements were initially developed with patient safety in mind, but evidence has accumulated that many lack outcome-specific support and have become barriers to care, particularly as third-party payers have increasingly used them to restrict access. Meanwhile, potent obesity management medications (OMMs) are prescribed with relatively limited oversight, often to individuals with preclinical disease, at costs that raise questions about economic sustainability. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission's distinction between preclinical obesity (excess adiposity with preserved organ function) and clinical obesity (a systemic illness characterized by objective organ dysfunction or substantial limitations of daily activities) provides a framework for evaluating current treatment access patterns. A critical implication of this framework, which warrants further exploration, is that it may narrow the population for whom medical treatment is considered necessary: for individuals with preclinical obesity, excess adiposity represents a risk state requiring monitoring and evidence-based counseling, not generally an ongoing illness requiring pharmacotherapy or surgery. This paper examines whether the current pattern, relatively low barriers to expensive, chronic pharmacotherapy for preclinical or early-stage disease; relatively high barriers to durable, cost-effective surgery for established clinical obesity, represents a departure from severity-matched care that warrants systematic reconsideration.

title: Comorbid Cardiovascular-Liver Disease Disparities: Current Understanding and Future Directions.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent chronic liver disease and a multisystem cardiometabolic disorder. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. This review examines disparities in the recognition and management of coexisting cardiovascular and metabolic liver disease. Shared metabolic and inflammatory pathways link liver disease with obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and CVD. Differences in measured disease prevalence across racial and ethnic groups must be interpreted separately from genetic susceptibility and in the context of structural inequities, diagnostic practices, and access to care. Socioeconomic disadvantage and sex- and gender-related barriers may further affect diagnosis and treatment. Resmetirom and semaglutide have expanded treatment options for selected adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), but unequal access to fibrosis assessment, insurance coverage, and longitudinal care may limit their benefits. An equity-centered cardio-hepatology framework should integrate early risk identification, stepwise noninvasive fibrosis assessment, individualized cardiovascular prevention, and access to indicated liver-directed therapies. Treatment and quality measures should reflect clinical eligibility rather than medication use alone. Inclusive research and coordinated long-term care are needed to evaluate whether these strategies narrow disparities.

title: Equitable Access to GLP-1 Receptor Agonists-Essential but Not Accessible.
Weight Loss Measurements Under the Microscope: How Type and Baseline Definition Shape Clinical Response After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery - A 2-Year Follow-up Analysis of 17,568 Patients.
abstract: In the era of modern metabolic-bariatric surgery, increasing attention is being paid to the assessment of clinical response after surgery. With the growing availability of multimodal obesity treatment, including preoperative pharmacological and lifestyle interventions, identification and optimization of factors associated with a suboptimal clinical response after metabolic-bariatric surgery (MBS) have become increasingly important.
